A Radical Proposal: Replace Hard Disks With DRAM

TLDR;

Experts suggests replacing a more permanent form of storage that retains data when powered off with a less permanent storage that erases instantly with power-off.

From a cursory scanning, no one who relies on data (i.e. everyone) will accept this "RAMcloud" unless it involves instant archiving to permament storage.

And how is this different from a disk cache? I'm surprised sometimes when my computer brings up a program instantly a couple of days after last use as opposed to running the program for the first time since boot. 8 Gb ram and spinning hard disks.

This is so hilariously ridiculous. SSDs are already limited by the SATA interface, which is why we have NVMe and M.2. We are already working our way toward SSD storage that's nearly as fast as RAM. Just using RAM instead is as stupid as Erin in The Office thinking that a disposable camera is for taking pictures and then throwing away without ever even developing them.

As @derkatalog said, this is nothing new. DRAM has been used for storage for years in the High IOPS business. Generally for large scale, highly available datastores. Hell in 2012, they were performing 1million iops on DRAM cards. These types of clustered storage systems, using DRAM (K2-D), NAND with Fusion-io PCIe flash cards, or hybrid DRAM NAND systems, have been around for years. The problem has been cost, not function.
It's cute how excited they get about these 'radical new ideas' which have been around for generations.

Certainly not a radical new idea to write an advertisement article promoting your own project either, and then report on it ostensibly as a unbiased observer. To Ousterhout's credit he did offer full disclosure on his connection to RAMCloud at the end, in the credits.

Hmm, why would anyone promote this, post-Snowden? In America, of all places, with its ISP Monopoly problem?

John Ousterhout is probably best known for creating the scripting language Tcl (Tool Command Language) while at the University of California, Berkeley. He then spent 14 years in industry. Returning to academia in 2008 as a Stanford professor, he realized that storage systems were not keeping up with networking. His response was a project called RAMCloud. “I’m weird among academics,” says Ousterhout. “I like to build systems that really work.”

Now this article makes sense

This is utter bullshit Yes, this uses nothing new. They speak of a "new architecture" but this architecture is nothing more than running a bank of DRAM for persistent storage while relying on HDD for constant backups. This is just an extreme ramdisk with 3x the backups. I also love how they glance over the face that DRAM is 100x more expensive than a standard HDD and 1000x faster. You can only use so much throughput, you can have a form of storage 10000000000000x faster than HDD and it won't mean shit because your bottleneck becomes the system (how fast can your computer understand data). NOW TAKE THAT KNOWING THIS IS A "CLOUD SERVICE"! Your bottleneck is your connection to the server. It is incredibly unlikely (as in there is no non-enterprise instance I can imagine and plenty enterprise instances I can't imagine) you will ever need speed like that for everything. AND no matter how fast DRAM is, if you can only download 1gb a second, your speed will not be more than 1gb per second!

Now, bottlenecks aside WHICH MAKES THIS SHIT STUPID AS FUCK. There is a matter of security. Do you know how fucked DRAM can get when you try to read an encrypted piece of data to and from it? ITS BAD. 99% of all computers read directly from DRAM for whatever purpose. Encryption ruins this by having to slow speeds in order to encrypt before data is read. On all computers even encrypted data is decrypted before it is read into DRAM. In a perfect world data would be decrypted before it was put into DRAM and encrypted as it hit persistent storage (HDD or SSD or otherwise). This means that the ram "cloud" will offer very little encryption for live non-backup data.

In summation, this product cannot offer you speeds more so than your local ISP and has the potential to be horribly insecure all while being janky as fuck. Thank you.
